How TO TARE A COLD BAT. no Wreinth.—The sea Son of the year is come when very many people who have ex- perienced pleasure and advantage from a doily cold bath have to discontinue the practice. Months will elapse before the return of geniol weather will allow of their indulgence in what nwy tie termed maris natural stimulant. Amongst the young and robust there are a large number who are able to bathe even in the depth of winter ; the advantage of no doing, is, however, questiooable. But let it be once well understood what a mid bath really ie, and the come by which we can avoid Scylla aud Charybdis will be obvious. A bath ie truly and really cold when it produces a cabal physiolcisaal ffect—a slight momenbory shuck followed by idea., red lasting reaction.' In answer to "Inquisitres,*. I may nay that caouteliorm, or , indiarubber, is the milky juice of a number of trees found : in Mexico, Central and South America, and in the East Indies. The tree is tapped in the morning, and during the : day a gill of fluid is received in a clay cup placed at each incision in the trunk. This is turned into a jsr, and is ready at once to be poured over any pattern of clay, the form of which it takes as auccessive layers are than applied. Ea drying and hardening are hastened by exposure to the smoke and beat Oft fire, and thus the substance acquires its ordi- nary black colour. lined by the sun alone it is white within and yellowish brawn without. When pure it is nearly colourlesa. Complete trying requirea several days' exposure to the sun. During this time the sebstance is soft enough to receive impressiona with • stick, and is thus ornamented , with various designs. The natives collect it upon balls of clay in the shape of bottles and various fanciful figures, in ! which shape it is often expo, ted.

At the adoption of the Fe,letal Cobtitutinn in 1787, and while it. ratification by the eeveral States was tinder discussion, the country W. divided into two parties—the Federalieta , headed by Washington and the elder Adams; and the anti- Federaliete, who afterwards took the name of Republicans, under the lend"rship of Jefferson and Mailisin. The Federalists were In favour nf a strong centralised Govern. meet ; the Republicans advocatid the sovereignity of the State, and the rights of the people, and finally secured I those additions and amendmehts to the Conetitution which were Intended to guarante" Rate rights, and which dr- dared that all powers not expressly granted to Congress , by the Constitution are retained by the States or the people. Haring the French Revolution and the ware which suceeethd it lb Fehiral party eympathised with England, while the Ite,teblieatin favoured the French, and being in parser, end, the presidency of Mr. Madison, declared war against England In 1812, a meanure which the Federalists violently opposed, going so far in the Hartford Convention as to threaten a ditwolution . . . .

The Whigs of 1840 repudiated alike tly principles and names of ,the Federalism. They profemed to be followers of Jeff,. son, and called themselves Democratic Whigs. Other party names met with in AmeriGn political writings are of a loctl, functienal, or temporary character. " Blue-light Federalist " was a name given to those who were believed to hoVO made friendly signals to British ships in the war of 1819. " ton Mes " and "Boat:tile " were old lictions of the Demo- cratic pantie, in New York, "Barn-burner "war applied an a term of reproach to a motion of the democracy supposed to be in sympathy with the "Anti-renters." The Belgian Chambers were opened on Tuesday by the King, who, in his speech horn the throne, thanked the people generally for the affectionate loyalty they displayed at the celebration of the fiftieth anniversary of Belgian indepen- dence. Alluding to the approaching marriage of the Prin. ce, Stephanie with the Crown Prince of Austria, hie Marsty said this event would crown all hie wishes." In referring to national affairs, the King stated that the harvest just gathered in had exceeded on the average that of pre. :ions years, ant the coridition of the public revenue had improvid. His Nlajesty closed his speech with the assur- ance that the Government would neglect no means of raising the mond and intellectual status of the people, and with that ohject would continue to etrengthen and develope public instruction in all grades, in conformity with constitutional principle.. . A correspondent of Nature, waiting from Tokio, Junin, givee some interesting particulars relating to the arrangement of the skin furrows of the hand. lie adopted the follnwin, method of observation A common slate or smooth board of any kind, ors sheet of tin, spread over very thinly and evenly with printer's ink is all that is required. The parts of which impressions are desired are pressed down steadily and softly and then transferred to slightly damp paper!' Each finger-tip may best be done singly and the ink may subsequently be removed by either hot water and soap or benzine. In the Japanese the lines on both thumbs form similar spiral whorls, and the fingers have peculiar ovals. The dominancy of heredity ie verystriking. l'nique patterns in a parent have been found to be repeated with striking fidelity in his child. Being sufficiently distinctive, impree- sions of finger marks may lead tot scientific identification of criminal% and farther, if unknown previously, heredity might evoke an expert to determine the relatives with con- siderable prolubility in some cases and with abzolote certainty in others. Bach. ease as that of the Tichborne claimant, it is suggested, might not be beyond the ranee of this principle. The whole subjemt is described an a rich anthropological mine for patient observers.

Tan Municipal Corporations Act be., in meet pule of the country. Wee on its trial for forty -four years. Neither Warrington nor Si. Helens—the only two local and adjscetit towns which have applied for and obtained charters of incorporation—have had eo long an experienee of the Aot hot both have had sufficient to dieelou imperfeetions that must won't or later claim the attention of the law-makers. In Warrington the Act has been in operation for a period of thirty-three pure, and, as we showed in the Examiner lent week, there exists the anomaly of we-third of the burgeeeee in the borough dictating land over-riding the other two-thirds in the govern- ment and •dininietration of the affairs of the manicipality. The town is divided into it.. ward.. Two of times wards oontaiu two-thirds of the elector., who only return to the Council Chamber twelve Councillors ; and the other three wards, inulzse* only one-third of the electors, who elect fifteen representative*. The borough of St. Helene, whit& wee incorporated in 1368, is, for municipal purlieus, divided into aix wards, and in all the wards there see 9,374 voters. Considerably more than one-half of this number meads hi two wards and return six CA -sod. lore, whilst the leerier half of the constituency I. eprend over four ward., and are repr vented by twelve . Councillors. Here, therefore, we have the anomaly of lees than one-half of the constituency electing two- thirds of theCennail and overridinguddictatitg to the majority, which has to hoc, nteet with one-third of the representation. This condition of things wines of the arrangement under the Act that no ward, how- ever much its populatiou may be enlarged or leeeened • by time, eau have an Increase or .liminetion of Councillors ; and that no ward cm be divided or tacked on to another without, in the trot instance, the approval of the ruling party in the Council, and, in the second induce, without the satiation of Parliament, which can only be had at great wet to the municipality. If municipalities are not the bed judge& of the arrangements that ought to exist for electing their own local governing authorities, Parliament is hardly like to be the beat body fee forming an opinion. What is needed is that Corporation. should be spared the wet and trouble of applying to Parliament for legislative suction to their

that they should themselves have the power—to form or change boundthies of wards, or if used be to increme the member of wards, to suit the requirement& of the [ creaaed or diminished population. ' partioular [ districts of boroughs, and so Nashse the repremuta- don in conformity with the changed condition of warda or localitie.. lu introducitig into the Rouse of Commons in 1835 the first measure of Municipal , Reform, the late Lord John Russell said, "Ii is, or I should be, the object of the Council, and one of its first objects, to replete/ant the town over which it I. plamd—to repreeent its property, to share in it. general feelings, and to take oare of its in. I rerwee, as haring that due convection which the governing body ought to nirintain with those who are liable to its burdens." Whilst we have the anomaly which at preeent enters ! into the Constitution of the Corporation of Werring- ! ton the object laid down by Lord Russell is but , imperfectly realised. The Act, however, as a was [ first draped by Lord Rumen and Lis friends, under- , went /mote °hang. by the heredittry legielators is the Upper Rouse of Perliaisent that Lord Brougham !declared it had been "rendered much worn, in their I lordships' hands." The original Bill provided that all the member. of the Council should be choice, by the bargemen, and that the Councillors ahould elect • Mayor from among themselves. Any barge.s wea to be eligible torn onuncillorehip, without, is sow, a property or pecuniary qualificialon. The hereditary legialeton introduced into the Bill the provision for the qualifieation • Town Councilke I. now required to poetess, and they required that Councillor, should sleet a Bench el Aldermen—• kind of superior grade of local legialators, who should not be subject to the whims and reprices of the bargemen The Bill &leo proposal that is boroughs which beds aeparate Bench of Magistrates Corporations should have the recommendation to the [ Crown ef persons euitable to to put upon the [ Conine ssion of the Peace. The lords refused to I tolerate each • proposal, and meek it out, though [ they were hunted by Lord Ili eugharn with " show- ing great mitered o the net Councils by refusing them the power which every Lord-Lieutenant of • ' county had at preeent—he meant the power Of recommending an individual to the Keeper of the Great Seel as that of a fit and proper person totes inserted in the Commission of the Puttee." Lord I Melbourne, the the. Prime Minister, contended for the retention of the prop/sal in the Bill, and the Rouse of Common, restored it. The Lords, however, dentinal to reverse their decision, anti by • majority of 62 they again etruek out the propmel, and it was eliminated from the Bill. Another question aff ectiag the Constitution of Muncipal Corporatione will arise for redrew 'wham- ever au attempt I. male to client • reform of the Municipal Corporation. Act. This question involves the preeent threefold arrangement which requires, at great inionvenience and at great cont, that every ward must have • number of Councillors divisible by three, and that one•third of the whole somber obeli leg elected mnually. The Act recognisee the fitness of representhtivee chicon by the burgeasee to hold ofilm for • period of three years, •nd yet, &heartily as we think, enjoins the burgeseme to annually undergo the excitement and expense of electing for a triennial period repreeentatives to manage their local public affair, Why • Town Council should not like Parliament be formed or elected all at owe thetead of by three inatalmente that nocemitate per- petual annual election, is herd to divine. Lord Melbourne's Cabinet, in framing the Bill, un- doubtedly introduoed the provision for the pressed system of constituting Corporstions by mould instal- ments ; but it would mom from some obeervations which fell from Lord John Rowell, upon whom rested, the duty of steering the Bill through the Houma of Commons, thth the Cabinet were not of one mind upon this particular point, and that to secure harmony end common action there wee • [inking of private opinion. on the part of a minority in the Cabinet. Lord Jahn Russell, in explaining the priuriples of the Bill, mid " We propose that menithrs of the Council shall be elected for three years, but that one third of them shall go out every year. Per my own part, I mut rimless my belief is that the inhabitant& of the towns, having aloe elected persona in whom they have me- fidenee, whether they elect them for three year. ore.. year, will generady elect the same persoth. They [ will lasi wally elect theme person, for whom they have • regard, sod to whom they believe rho clispcio4l and mmagement of their property may her/defy entrusted, aid whom they will not lightly think of changing. But, prowiding that there shell hose annual electios [ of only one-third of the Council, we shall Lars it

leant two-thlrda of We Council who will have had some experience of the management of towns." Tha fear of evil arising, if there were not meml.mrs kept in the Conned with at least one or two yearn' ex- perience of municipal affairs when an annual election canto about, won no ill grounded as the idea would be that netional affairs would sink into chaos unless rarlientert woe elected by inetaiments, after the man- ner of Municipal Corporatione. The preftnt muni- cipal electoral machinery is too complicated and contly, and the absurdity of having a triennial local parlia- ment, constituted by three annual elections, is attended with inconveniences and disadvantages that are neither neoeesary nor warranted. If it were desirable to further demonetrete the absurdity we might point to the fact that whilst towns are burdened with an election of commillors every year to sit for three years, it ix deemed miflicient within the corporate circle to go through the bultincee of electing aldermen only once in three years and then to put aldeemen us °aloe for six yearn. These are anomalies that must ere long be removed, and the wonder is that they ehould have been tolerated for the number of years they have been.

Whilst on this subject, it is perhaps worth while pointing out —seeing that in the agitation for leesen- ing drunkenness suggestions aro thrown out for the formation of benchon of magistrates and Mimicipal Corporations into licensing boards—that in the Mosicipal Corporations Bill, 1835, there was neloune providing that Town Councils or committees of Town Councils should have the power of granting alehouse Boons.. The hereditary legislators, however, struck the aim., out when the Bill canto before them, and the old system of licensing the drink traffio was perpetuated.

fIIELAND is undoubtedly just now on the verge of a revolution, and mooch tact and determination will have to be exercised by the Government to euppreen, without the lose of blood and life, the angry feelings which member,' of the Land League in the West, and Orangemen in the North, ere displaying towards each other. We have more than once contended in these celeinne that the tenantry of Ireland have suffered and borne wrong* under unjust and cruel laws too lolur, and that they have had much to exas- perate them to opeely clamour over their grievances. But the length to which the fomenters of disaffeetion ill the Sister Isle have gone is warrauted neither by the operation of oppreesive laws nor by common sense. The members of the Land League, and more especially it, leaders sod agitators, are out ignorant of the fact that the Government now in power have not only shown that they fully realise the unsatisfac- tory relations subsisting between the landlords and the tenantry of Ireland, but that they have made, and are willing to agaiL make, en effort tone amend the statutes as will give greater security of tenure to tenant., and enjoin on the part of landlords a practical recognition of improvemetee effected by temente, who have not reaped full advantage of theme improve. meats. But this protein° of amelaainect of the laws, which would be satiafying to meet people, is insufficient for Mr. Denial and his reefr, res who work the wires of the Land Leagues; and tile result in that we have now • reign of terror in Ireland, in tome parts of which no respect ic shown for animate uor inanimate proper- ty, nor are the lives of persons who dare to set the de- cream of the Land League at defiance, worth a day's purchase. The revolutionary feeling promoted and teetered by the Land League will delay rather than hasten the accomplishment of the design:Le the leaders of the Land League meek to achieve. The first duty of a government is to inlaid upon the obeervance of such laws so exiiit, notwithstanding that them law. may be cruel and oppreseive in their character ; and whilat the attention of the Government is taken up with the nuppremitiin of auarchy, and with enforcing an obeervenee of rotor, it in hardly likely that the Government can devote its attention to the considera- tics of stetuten the, requi.so amendment in order to establish greater cipiity and juatice. The firm atti- tude shown by tier Majesty's Government in taking proceedings on a charge of conspiracy against some of the mere prominent leadere of the Land League, and in ferwarding troops to prevent the enraged Orangemen of the North, marching to the relief of Captain Bycott, and the disaffected member. of the Land League Dem coming into collision, boo evoked from maey of our Irish friends a condemnation of the Government. Already we hear of meetings of excited electors, not only in the Sister Isle, but in England. proclaiming their hostility to the prelent Government, though it him proved t o be to them the most friendly of say Gevernments that have held the seals of office before it. The Government, under no cir- onmstancee, can permit the disaffected tenantry of Ireland to sofa, take the law into their own hands aa to make them • terror to the whole country ; and, assured of thla, our discontented Iriih neighbour. uhould not overlook the fact that they are likely to get mere favours from the present Administration than from any that will succeed it of a Conservative character, If by the action of the Irish electors, or thriaugh some other canoe, a Coneervistiv• Government should supplant the pretest Glad.. stone Administration, our Irish friends will find that with the Conservatives in office they will meet with different tree talent to that which has been extended to them by the preeent Government. • Coneervative Adosinietration would not hesitate to attempt to pews the preeent rebellious sod di.ffeeted feeling in Ireland by the application of coercive measures and by military eepionage. Martial law would not bring increased happiness to the country, nor will a Cos- eervative Government seek to appease the impatience of the people by an effort to pees eueh meamuree RA the Irish Compenaatinn Disturbance Bill and the Irish Registration Bill, both of which were rejected hut ...mien by the Upper House of Parliament. It ix about time mar Irish friend. sores, the water stayed their hands in keeping up a reign of terror, and that they b..gen to out:wider whether they ere not delaying the enactment of jest laws for Ireland, end whether it is net more likely that they will receive greater favours at the hande of the present Governmerit than they would be likely to wring from a Conservative Government, where fleet stop would be the suspension of the Habeas Corps- Act and the exerche of most rigid enactments that would cripple the lamely the people of Ireland new here.

I , The debate on the tnotion of the hon. member for Tars° that the present Education Acts should be amended so as, to give p,wer to school attendance committeee to erect , schools where addnional accommodation is required, with- out being obliged to incur the expense of establishing , school boards ; ands:so in the interests of religious liberty to remove a:I restrictions at present exieting in the Welling of religion in elementary achool., was resumed by the hon. member for Wnsrmara, sho opposed the motion, and in the course of his speech, said no one objected to religious teaching so long as it did not partake of dogma. tin far from toeing anything by the present state of affair., they prithd theniselves upon the fact that their religious institutions were far in advance of those of any other country. (A(plause.) it. hoped the exial sys- tem Of the country would not he split op simply because it was pretended one religion was pre-eminent above another. (Appian.). As to the religion, junction, he did not think children would split many haire upon theological dif- • ferences, but if they implanted in their minds the groat principles of religion, that was all they needed to Cu, for at present. (Hear, bear.) lie thought education would be far mere illuminated through such means, and he hope,l that to the many glories of the crown there would be added another , that llm sceptre of our monarch was swayed over an educated people. (Applause.) The hon. member for Wines aupported the motion. The HowsSecseragr contended that to look upon the qnestion simply as a question of expense was false and de.. Waive. If they vested the power sought by the motion in town councils they would have the same excitement at elections. But the Board of Education had been informed ',that after two or three elections all the animosity which first existed died out, and matters had been arranged to theutas- faction and comfort of everybody concerned." As to the " religion. liberty " mentioned in that .notion, if ever there me a patmly on words it was exhibited in this case. By religious liberty was meant the exercise of their own con- victions, bat the gentle.inen of the Opposition wanted . .

to teach their own dogma in the rrpublic school.. (Applause.) He cared very little by what moans the education of children wall brought shout provided it was . brought about. (Heat, hear.) the hoped to see the time when statesmen in England would see it to he their duty and the duty of s great country like this to make provision I no that every child born within its borders 'Mould he edu. cated at the expense of the State. (Applause.) He also hoped to see the time when it would be possible for the child of a poor man who developed talents of A high order to pass through the universities without the detriment of I the great expense at present extsting. (Applause.) When ! that was done their highest hopes would he realised. (Ap- plauxe.) The hon. member for DAVENPORT said that in hie opinion I whatever was the creed of,, child its educdion ahould lie provided for, and tithe parents of a child were not posses.' of a creed he would treat the opinions of those parents with the highest respect. (Hear, hear.) He thought Town , Councils were eminently fitted to deal with the Elaine, and if the resolution were adopted the matter would he dealt with more wisely and much more econonticAly than other-1 , wise.

—Tire right boa. member for NOB-MAMMON said that were they to spend tome money in education they would spend leea in providing gaols and policemen. (Hear, hear.) ing with the latter part of the motion, he mid Hut all that Secularist@ required was that they should please themselves ,as to how their children should be brought up. The Bible should be kept out of day schools entirely. ("No, no.") He thought hon. members would varcely agree to the remarks he might make, Until religion was to be taught in the schools he would ask as a parent, what religion P The right hon. gentleman then proceeded to Aeal with the vari- : ous religions, and declared that if religion was to be taught by a gentleman who subscribed to the 39 Articles of the Church of England he would make hie child an inhuman monster.

Thetron.member for Mwernose thought the hon. gentle- man who intrnduced the question admitted that the conscience clause should be maintained. He thought the right hon. member for Northaotpton was wandering from the subject. (Hear, hear.) The hon member for Tare, I think the conscience clause will prevent hie children from becoming" inhuman monsters." (Applause.) .

The right hot';;;11;ber for Notrrnsargrow said the con- science clause did not prevent his children being potted at in the school. (Hear, hear.) Ile held that the day school was the place where children should he fitted for this world, where no spesplative notions should he taught, and where what had been accepted as troth by men all round should be taught to children. He held that religion should he taught at home, And that the parents example and religion should he the religion taught to a child. (Hear, hear.) . . . .

The hon. member for the BORDER &BOWS liked the idea of baying the education of their children in the hands of a lord, of gentlemen eelected by the ratepayer.. He heard the hon. member for Truro cry out for mote religions liberty. The Nonconformiste had cried out for it for 300. yearn, end he waa delightedte find that aorneone else would join with them in seeking religious liberty all over the world. (Applause.) But hewn. afraid the motion did not mean all it said. It was no qnestion of religion. liberty. What they wanted was a particular privelege which the Noncon- formists denied them. The members of the Opposition simply wanted to educate for their own party purpo.e. (Applause.) He went he for pure unwctarian teaching in every school • in the country. (Appletate.) ANNUAL TEA PARTY AND BALL. On Monday lest the annual tea pertv and ball of the Orangemen of Warrington, wm held at the Public Hall, to celebrate and keep in homer the birth of William the Third of glorious and pious memory," also in aid of the widows and orphan's fund in connection with the institution, when upwards of 300 permns net down to • euhetantial tea. Ihe Iroom was gaily decorated for the occasion with emblems of the order, and the society's banner was suspended at the rear rof the room. After tee. short meeting was held presided i over by Bro. Councillor Richard Kern. past provincial greed I master for the North-Western per.mnee of England, also I past district master of Warrington: and le was supported on the platform by the following distio.mished brethren Bro. tine. Foster, deputy chairman of the Conner-retire Amociation of Penketh F time. Bloomfield, W.M., J. Mather, W.M. and B.la diatiict secretery, Musgrave,Croley, B. Johnson, di,trict treasurer ;Jno. Roberts, Imstee; Oswald Brookes, D. M.'; Thom. Edgar, secretary, Spencer, W.M., Unsworth, W.M ; W Iliarn Crow, D.M. ; Wright, DM.; j Hough, OM.: 11111, eecretery Cooper, It The Cueturen, after thanking them for the honour thee bad done him in constituting him chairman of that meeting, mid they were met there that evening to commemorate the birth of hing William the Thinl, prince of Orange. It might be asked what was there connected with the birth of Rio, William, that they should hold each an important Igathering, especially •hen he lived WO yeare ago. Why It seemed to him an important as evw it was The greatnem of that man had been handed down from one generation to another, and the work he performol and the lawe th. estab- lished were still doing their work. In IWO when King William wee ho, o Hier, was great rejoicing aa it wee believed that the son if spared would work wonders in the fond. Ile wee carefully and studimely watched in the dem of big youth, and he gave early signs of great abilit• and aptitude. Ste was fond of reading God's holy word, and that bock beceme • book of great importance to him, and lie learnt lessons from it how to frame law., lemons how to govern, and they were reaping the fruits of his wisdom to that very day. He paseed the Toleration Act, which enabled all to wotallip in their own way non fashion. In 1688 lie was called to the throne,and She whole acts of hie life were directed in the petting down of tyranny anol oppression, end te bringing about such laws as would lead to the good government of the country. His aim was realic and truly to mtablisb the British Constitu- tion mto dm basis. Ilia motto was! The liberties of England I wilt 11111i1.1111, and no surrender." It had gone abroad that the I range body were a sort of tyrannical people, but there was not a word of truth in it. That heti- lotion was not aggresaive ; it wee defensive, but they would not allow their privileges to be trampled down with impu- nity, end they would not allow any concession whereby the libertiesof England might be injured, ore stain brought mmn their religion. sA short time ago he Am e letter in one of the local ',int, that it RN likely he (Mr. Kean) amid be made NLIVOr of Warrington. Another letter ap- peared saying that he need not anticipate that until he re- lirmoished the Orange body, and the writer of that letter bail the audacity to rgn bin name" Liberty." The chief magistrate of that borough should he amen of even balance, straightforward in everything lie did, and a man 1115ott whom the people could rely anti look our to. He thought the time had come when the o.rangemi-n of this c.untry should make themselves more promment in great queetions. There wan en election short time ago—a parietal election—and they euffered defeat. That defeat, however, vas one they need not be afraid of. It was one of those defeats that if the same means had been Mi.. in Warrington as were taken in Chester the results would torn leen similar. (Laughter, They lived to witness the view, ies of their opponents, but at the ailllC time they witnessed name of their tricks to achieve victory. Now, he would he defeated rather-than use trickery and deceit Ile hod always endeavoured to come before tbou with sober mind and conscience, and that he did not go away without speaking his mind irrespective of creed or party. It was said that the Oran., hmly were dying out, but thought it net, never stronger than it was at the present time. Their lady was strong in Ireland. He believed that on account of the ingeno ity of the pteeent Government they would have to call Ole Orangemen to help them in Ireland. When it came to • question of low sod order, the Orangemen were put to the front and trusted. They were a loyal body, and obliged logo when celled upon. They bad saved hundreds and thoumnds of livea and large quantities of property in times gone by. He hop that soon their body would be augmented in Warrington. He ensured them the time was coming when, with the en- croachtnents at home and abroad, they would have to forcibly adopt the motto of King William, and my, The Protestant religion I will niaiotain, and no eon-ender." (qr.'s)

Bro. Fosree, after referring to their constitution in England, (Yid that they wore likewiee strong In Ireland. They had go d room le join and band themselves together bec;uise they had strong foea to meet. The thange body were not satia&el with the Governnient Of the country 05 it wee being carried on, particularly in relation to matters re- ferring to Ireland. At the present thee there was an agita- tion going on in Ireland. which wan supported by what was called Home Rulers. The Government ought not simply to discourage that agitation, but to put it dawn at once. The question of land in Ireland was no question, for dis- 'urbane. had taken place there for generations past. It could not he a question of religion for the simple reason that everyone in Ireland had • right to eerve God after their own fashion The interest , of Ireland had loeen grossly neglected by the British POOl iO. meet. Mr. Gladstone committed the greatest injoetice tin- ned when he destroyed the /Bah Church, and then he gave them • sort of lend bill, following that up by placing nearly the whole of the education of the country M the hands of Roman Catholics. Thirty years ago there woe no cause of compLtint in Ireland, and since that lilllo Mr Gladstone had been giving them "Ineenagee of peace." What they , blamed r he Government boron. that during the Late electoral eampaign they stirred up the seeds of discord in Ireland. Mr. Gladstone "stumped " the .untrv, and hie cry was, "teen Oct the Government," " Ireland lot the Irish ." and the interesting unlit of these carpet-bag oratore was that their purpose was suited, and they got imp power. The moment the Liberals were in power the agitators began to cry torn settlement of the land question in Ireland. All that was the outgrowth of the etatements mode by Mr. Gladstone and other Liberals during the last election. They raiaed the storm, and now they had not courage to quell it. ((tear. hear.) 3he present Government dare not ‘. tackle "1 the grievances in Ireland, and when they would be settled no one knew. (Applause.) Alderman CoOg had great pleasure in propoeing that Alderman Harrison be appointed Mayor for the coming year. He had served the town for a great number of years —a number of years lo the capacity of chairman of the Health Committee—and previous to that to. had served on the Hoard of Commissioners. He was quite sure he wee a gnat h man in whom they could place • good deal of trust and confidence. If. lieZl pleasure in propostng him, as he was a gentleman who could sustain the dignity of the office in a proper manner. Alderman R.I. had pleasure in ecconding the resolu- tion, as he thought Alderman Harrison was eminently fitted for the ottice. The motion was then put and carried unanimously. The mover anti seconder of the resolution then went out of the Council Chamber into the committee-room, In which Alder- man Ilarri.on had been 10.sted during the first part of the proeeedings. On entering the room he was received with cheers . .

Ablerthin Harrison then seated himself in the aivic chair, and the hx..Mayor ptawl around his neck the chain of honour, adding, "1 hive now invested you with this chain of office, and, as I raid before, I wish you every healtls and happiness." The Ex- Mayor then took, seat by the silo of Colonel Gamble. The newly-elected Mayor, having made the usual deelirations, "wearing ttne allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Victoria," and that in the office if Mayor be would endeavour to die. charge hie duties w without fear or favour," thanked the Couucil for Om honour they had conferred upon him. He was sure he toll deeply the 1100, or in being unanimously elected to the distinguished position of Mayor of St. Helens, and he would endeavour to do hia duty in the Council faith- fully and imp:it'll illy. lie hoped he knew the responsi- hilitiee resting upon him, and be would rely upon their genet°. indulgence and co-operation in the execution of hia duty, and if it pleased Almighty Hod to spare his health during Isis term of office it should he his desire to fulfil his duties and maintain the dignity of the chair. He might ray that it watt his intention to attend Divine envies at the Parish Church on Sunday, and he should be glad to have the company of all those who could make it convenient to attend. Ile thanked them very much (Cheers.) He had alai to announce that he had great pleaaure in appointing Mr. Alderman Johnson Deputy Mayor for the coming year. (Applause.)

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. -- IMPORTANT MEETING. The monthly meeting wsa held on Tueeday, Major Cross presided, and there were also present—Menem. Carey, Wells, Brown, rankhurst, Hey, Gasket!, Knight, Foster, Matthews, Barrow, teenage, Beasley (law clerk ), Robert. (engineer), Iligginson (surveyor), Allen (accountant I, and Dickson inspector). THE VACANCT ON THE 141AHD. After the reading and confirmation of the minutes, . The Camara.; said the first business was to fill up the vacancy caumd by the resignation ol Mr. J. L. Muspratt. Mn. Watts raovol that the Board should not exercise • their power to fill up the vamucy, as in the ordinarytoaree of things Mr. Muspratt would have retired in Manchester, but leave the selection of a gentleman to the general body of the ratepayers. 'rt. CHAIRMAN thought that before the motion was put to the Board he ought to read a communication, dated the 3rd net, which he had received from the Widom l'roperty and ItatepAyers' Association, in reference to the resignation. ill which they suggested that Mr. Samuel Sadler, of Lugs-. dale-road, elmuld be elected to the position. Mr. BARROW seconded the motion, which woe passed tuanimously. rue SCHOOL HOARD •NO THE merrsa.” A letter was read from Mr. U. IL Ihinhy, dated the 28111, October, in reply to one from the Law Clerk, dated 27th September, stating that his communimtion had that day been laid before the meeting of the School Board, who were ' Of opinion that the letter reCeiVed from Mr. Carey (which has previously been given in our col Lunn.) on the fair gum.' tion, was a private one to himslf (Mr. Carey).

raaNIVoRTII AND ITS MAMMA, ACCOMMODATION. Two lettrre, dated the 16th and 20th ult., were read in I answer to the application of the Board to the Sheffield and 1 Midland Company for increased railway accommodation at Farnworth. The replies stated that if the directors acceded to the wishes of the Board, it would render it necessary for them to open another junction and put on two additional signalmen, and the receipts from the Motion would not rennburse them for much an expenditure. The Cnatuven felt pretty core that the disinclination of , the railway company to the scion In this matter aroge from want. of will, and not from • fear of extra expenae to which they would be put as a consequence of acceding to the wiffies of the BOAnl. ftc Kara an inetance, and Said he might quote several others, with the abject of allowing that this woe the case. The other morning he was at the War- rington station, and he saw two express trains go past within ten minutes of each other, and he could not see any reamn why one of them should not have stopped at Farnworth to allow of the collection of tickets.

The Gas an I Water Contenitiene minutes stated that the roof timbers were being put in place at the Netherly engine house, arid the chimney shaft had been taken a height of WI feet. The laying of the water pipes for Ditton-road would be proceeded with as soon as they had been tested. The Water delivered during the four weiiks ending October 20th, showed an increase of 18'8 this year as compared with 1679. The gas eent out during the four weeks ending the 20th ult., showed an increase of 201 per cent for this year. A minute bad been passed showing the proposed arrange- ment of rails and crossings at the liitton gas yard, in con- nection with the Sheffield and Midland branch railway about to la. constructed along the northerly boundary of the yard, but only on the understanding that the line between the easterly and westerly boundries of the Board's land he atoll times kept clear and left open. Resolved that a strip of land, 18 feet in width, along and the full length of the easterly elde of the Board's land, be conveyed to them as compenutinn for the land to be appropriated by the committee for their raile. That the points and crossings in connection with the branch be put in and tnaintained by the ! committee. Recommended, on re-consideration of the nub- ject, that consumers of water by totter let Ditton and otaer out-townships be charged an additional fire per cent on the scalerates as charges to meter consumers being ratepayers in Widnes. The IAl• clerk reported that the Lancashire Telephone Co. repudiated the Edison Cu',. agreenient, and , that the latter company was in liquidation. Instructions had, therefore, been given to the engineer to have the Matra-. ments at the gm works and accountant's office, put in order by some out side party. Recommended that the application of the plumbers employed by the Board for an increase of wages, be not entertained. it; further discussion had taken place on the subject of Mr. Timmen Strck's well heading • contract.

Mr. F. li. Gowan& in proposing the adoption of the minutes, with certain exceptions, said that the minute aa to , the plan of the rails' arrangement at Ditton gas yard could not be dealt with that day, and he shonhlAsk them to refer it , back to the committee. The law clerk reported that counsel's opinion had not yet been taken as to the proposal about the suggested increase of charge for snpplying water to Ditton. A long letter ha I come to hand from Mr. rimming, as to the Stock's well contract, with three alternative schemes which would require the attention of the comin tee, but which if they we-e t, attempt to deal with that day would occupy • great deal ef the time of the Board. He should, therefore, move that this matter he left in the hands of the committee. Ile considerwl that a fitting optewtunity for saying a few words about the property of the corn- , mitten Ile thought they vrould all agree with hint that the Board might be heittily congratulated upen their foresight and numbness of action at the farm. itme—more particularly with regard to the water. Like all eendstone wells, their Stocks.weli was not yielding as much as it did at one time, and, if they bid to rely upon it at present, it could not eupply them with the qua.dity of water they re- quired. Consequently, it most be quite evident to every member of the Board that they did not erect their Netherley and other stations any too soon. This was shown to a very great extent by the increased sale of water. The increasel per month, in per centages, varied extremely. The eon. I sinuous average monthly increased sale of water over the hist nine months was 171 per cent. Anyone with the slightest knowledge of the matter would at once see where the Board would now have been if they had no: lwen able to claim a good supply of water from Netherley. Of course when they got all their engines to wnrk the increased supply of water would be very great. Ile believed that if they bad to go to Netherly to day for the purpose of buying land, they could scarcely obtain it for such purpose at any price, lie would Next notice the gas works. lie believed that all the money spent at those works had not been ex- pended one minute too soon, and that there had not be,n,l en the slighteat degree, any extravagance in carrying out those extensions. The continuous average monthly in- crease in the sale of pa over the last nine month', was 171 percent., which eras an extremely satisfactory state things, and sloowed that if they had not made the extonsion• at the works at the time they did, they would not have been able to supply the quantity of gas now required hy Widnes. In conclusion, the streaker said he had spoken to several engineers with whom he was acquainted, and they bad ex- ' premed their opinion that the amount paid loy the 'Board for the Mations at Netherler and Bellevale were ridiculously . .

"Me. Bnoww seconded the motion, with the euggested alterations, and remarked that the Local Government Board , had congratulated tem Board on carrying out the earl.. extensions of their works at the time they did. Me could quite support whr,t Mr. Gossage heal said with reference to , the gas works, which he believed oh, worked in • very , satinfactory manner. As far as he had had an opportunity , of judging, and comparing the cost of “rrying on their I work, with the suma expended at other places, he had come to the conclusions that instead of paying more for manufac- turing gee, they were paying rather lee,. Mr. GossAot wished to mention out further fact, and this was that although they now depended tot their supply of water upon wells, they were perfectly safe in no donne until the Vyrnevy scheme was carried out, when they would receive that supply from the Liverpool Corporation which wee guaranteed on the passing of their late Act. The minutes were passed.

The Highway. Building, md Stet Committee made the following recommendations •—That the Local invernment Board be asked to allow £OOO of the atnount sanctioned for Church-street. Farnwerth, to be used for Pit-lane. That the osrneoftl,alo.trnrntioneotthocooghfate be changed to St. Lakes-road. That the Surveyor prepare an estimate to be laid before the Board of the cost of the proposed alteration. in Pit-lane. That instructions be given to him to subniit to the owners an estimate for cleanalnmEliaabeth-street, and obtain from each an order for the work, which shell not be andertaken unless all comply. That Instructions he given to .11 Mr. McClellan'a attention to thedangerousconditton of the roof and • portion of the wall of the old North of Eng. land Works at Lugadale, and to request hint to make them rife. That the Kent-street crossing be paved. Mr. BRIG!, moved that the minutes be approved, and referred to the auggestion as to the experditure of £5OO for Pit-lane. He remarked that this we.. mutter which had been before the Board for more than two yearn, and arrange- ments had been entered into with varlet, people, condi- tional upon the improvements being carried out. Mr. CAREY proposed that the minutes h:adopted, and re- marked that the navigation of the Mersey was in an unsatia-. factory state. FANCY FAIR AT WARRINGTON. ' Among the many ancient buildings existent in and abont the borough of Warrington, the Church of St. Janes'. Latch• ford, may certainly be numbered. Externally it premnts a very modern appearance, as time aa dently dealt with it in a favoured way, but its interior arrangements are not of that excellence to be seen in our more modern churches. There may be seen the puritani.l high-backed pew, where • pretentious worshipper may with impunity indulge inc power . nap " with his fellow wor- shipper, or play the Lame gem° but in a different fashion With himself. What should tine broad aisle up the centre of the church leaf the present time Monet filled with a miserable array of free benches, leaving two •ieles along the sides of Filch inadequate proportions that the silken attired lady who perchances to arrive at church late on • Sunday morning, mume the ettention of the whole con- gregation by the rustling of her brocade. The gallery ie of the primitively heavy and uncomfortable description, and requires to be thoroughly remodelled, if not altogether ex- tingenthed. At one time the number of worshippers at this church wan relatively large, and the moo nmodation too- yided was only just adequate to more the deinends for space, but of late years, from some came or other, probably intes- tine, the congregation has diminished in • very perceive. degree, until. at the preeent time, the &treaders on divine worship can he comfortably mated in the body of the church, and the gallery tine been proscribed. Thie state id things hal eines the induction of Ile Rev. T. Slater into the living connected with this church, occupied his eerie. at- tention, and also the attention of the churchwardens, and it war felt that if the church wee to be made comfortable end internally agreeable, a complete rectification of its existing arrangements was highly desirable. To enable them to carry out this resch the view, along with his churchwardms, applied to the Chancellor of the diocese for a faculty to enable thetn to pull down the gallery, and reonlel the centre of the church. After sone delay a faculty one obtained, and the cost of the proposed alteratione will be about g 3,000. It is not the inten- tion of the churchwarden. to carry into operation the pro- posed seheme at once, but to ge to work gradually and surely, so that the church will not be encurnnered with • heavy debt. Churches in need of money ievariably resort to bmaars as a mode of clearing off a pecuniary incubus, or of raising money to carry on some work, and in this cam • somewhat similar proceeding has been token. The willing hands and heorte of the congregerion were applied to, and it wax resolved to get up what is known am a fancy fair. It was considered that this would prove a greater attraction than the old.faehioned hatear, and the eubsequent procee'.. inge showed that the juidgment of the prmumers ems nor ill-founded. The ladies—ever willing in a cone like the present one—eet to work at once, and in procese of time • surprising quantity of goods were made and collected. and . ve fancie faire" proved a emcees.. Last Tuesiey, the feir ! was opened at the Drill Hall under very auspicious circum- stances—fine weather and the patrontee of ae.erOU. public. The decorations were of the highest character, and reflected great credit on all concerned. The arrange,nents were admirable, and this neatness and order wm at once apporent fox person on entering the room. Everything to secure taste with effect, aril the titular morying eut of the scheme had been done with a praiseworthy result. In the generous enthusiasm which prevailed on the aubject the ex- pectation. of the moat sanguine promoter had been exceeded he the title could hardly be borne out without soena fanciful arrangement. were introduced, the old-fonhioneel ealle were dispensed with, and erection. more pleasing to the eye and taste were made. Thus one Mall partook of the character of : . au " Eaetern Bizaar," with o.iental accompanimenic another was denominated the " House that Jack built ", • and others were called the " House of Cards," "Banbury Croes," .• The Ship."" Sir,—The succession of unfavourable mason.. .he partial failure of most crops this year—notably of the barley and green crops—and the unremunerative pricesolnain,d by far- mers for their produce, combine to render the prosp,cts of Agriculturists gloomy and discouraging.
